claims.text: Pulumi published a blog post titled "SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi" at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/.
The blog post at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ provides a closer look at the engine mechanics behind SST's migration to Pulumi.
SST (Serverless Stack) originally used AWS CDK as a starting point for its infrastructure tooling.
AWS CDK ties infrastructure to AWS.
Debugging SST's CDK-based infrastructure was frustrating due to CloudFormation templates.
Multi-cloud deployment was nearly impossible for SST when built on AWS CDK.
Pulumi lets SST offer a faster, more flexible, and provider-agnostic infrastructure experience.
SST was originally built on top of AWS's Cloud Development Kit (CDK).
AWS CDK allows developers to define their infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.
With CDK and CloudFormation, the infrastructure code is a code generator that produces an intermediary format (such as YAML or JSON) that is then executed to deploy resources.
With CDK and CloudFormation, the code a developer writes is not the same as the code running during the deployment process.
AWS CDK has an AWS-centric nature that limits its use outside the AWS ecosystem.
AWS CDK supports only AWS for multi-cloud/provider support.
Pulumi supports AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-premises infrastructure.
AWS CDK debugging is hard due to CloudFormation.
Pulumi provides real-time debugging.
AWS CDK supports only TypeScript and Python as languages.
Pulumi supports any programming language.
AWS CDK deployment speed is slower due to CloudFormation.
Pulumi has faster deployment due to direct execution.
AWS CDK is hard to trace errors with, providing poor visibility.
Pulumi provides clear deployment state visibility.
AWS CDK's extensibility is limited to the AWS ecosystem.
Pulumi supports custom providers and workflows for extensibility.
AWS CDK uses a CloudFormation state file for state management.
Pulumi uses Pulumi-managed state for state management.
AWS CDK supports secrets management only through AWS Secrets Manager.
Pulumi supports cross-cloud secret management.
Pulumi treats infrastructure code as a first-class program executed directly during deployment, rather than generating an intermediary format.
With Pulumi, the infrastructure code running during deployment is the same code the developer wrote.
Pulumi's provider-agnostic approach allows the SST team to work with a wide range of cloud and on-premises platforms.
Pulumi provides improved visibility and debugging capabilities, as described on the Pulumi Insights product page (https://www.pulumi.com/product/pulumi-insights/).
Pulumi provides built-in extensibility features such as custom providers and dynamic components.
Pulumi supports defining infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Go, or C#.
Pulumi allows deploying infrastructure across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and on-premises environments from one consistent workflow.
Pulumi offers more advanced deployment workflows, documented at https://www.pulumi.com/docs/pulumi-cloud/deployments/.
Pulumi provides better visibility into the deployment process, as described at https://www.pulumi.com/product/pulumi-insights/.
Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS simplifies "day one" tasks, as described in the AWS guide at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/.
Pulumi offers an on-demand workshop titled "Getting Stated with Infrastructure as Code on AWS" at https://www.pulumi.com/resources/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws/.
Pulumi offers upcoming Platform Engineering or DevOps workshops listed at https://www.pulumi.com/resources/#upcoming.
Users can sign up to try Pulumi at https://app.pulumi.com/signup.
SST is a framework that makes building modern full-stack applications on your infrastructure easy.
SST's Ion is the code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications.
SST Ion's constructs (or components) are deployed using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation (CFN).
Once SST's Ion engine is stable, it will be released as SST v3.
SST leverages Pulumi behind the scenes for its providers and deployment engine.
SST bridges Terraform providers through Pulumi.
SST (Serverless Stack) makes money primarily through its managed service called SST Console.
The SST Console is optional and includes a free tier.
SST primarily relies on SaaS revenue through its managed platform, with potentially supplemental income streams like enterprise services and consulting.
SST v3 replaced AWS CDK with an embedded Pulumi engine.
SST v3 bridged Terraform providers.
SST v3 dropped AWS CDK for an embedded Pulumi engine that talks to Terraform-bridged providers.
Using SST v3's embedded Pulumi engine requires no Pulumi account.
When SST rebuilt its deployment engine for v3, it did not write a new engine from scratch.
`sst deploy` runs on an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the actual cloud API calls.
`sst deploy` requires no CDK.
`sst deploy` requires no CloudFormation.
`sst deploy` requires no Pulumi account or Pulumi Cloud dependency.
Nitric runs application deployments through the Pulumi engine rather than building its own diff, state, and provider layer from scratch.
Defang runs application deployments through the Pulumi engine rather than building its own diff, state, and provider layer from scratch.
SST's team's public attention has broadened to include an AI coding agent called opencode.
SST is still shipping as of this writing.
SST v3 is the framework's Ion-based rewrite.
SST v3 replaced AWS CDK and CloudFormation with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls.
Running `sst deploy` needs no separate Pulumi install.
Running `sst deploy` needs no Pulumi account.
The Pulumi engine ships inside the SST CLI.
SST keeps state in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account.
The SST team has repeatedly stated, since the rewrite shipped, that SST's architecture is built on the Pulumi engine as described in this post.
SST is an open source TypeScript framework, from the team formerly known as Serverless Stack, for building and deploying full-stack applications to AWS and more than 150 other providers.
SST users define their app's infrastructure and code together in a single `sst.config.ts` file, using SST's own components (functions, queues, buckets, static sites, and so on).
`sst deploy` handles the provisioning end to end.
Through 2023, SST's provisioning layer was built directly on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
In late 2023 the SST team began a rewrite, code-named Ion, that replaced SST's entire deployment layer.
Ion shipped as SST v3 in mid-2024.
SST v3 (Ion) has been the only supported SST architecture since it shipped in mid-2024.

SST's blog post "Moving away from CDK" states: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)."

SST's blog post "Moving away from CDK" states: "When you run `sst deploy`, those resources make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls to create your resources."
SST's docs page "What is SST" states: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi."

Gautier Blandin, in "Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis," wrote: "SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood to manage and provision resources, and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to using SST's constructs, enabling resources with no associated SST constructs to still be defined and deployed."
Kiryl Anoshka, in "SST ditches AWS CDK. Time to move on to Ion," wrote: "You may notice right away the imports from Pulumi. It means the whole deployment process will be built on Pulumi now."
The published `package.json` for SST's platform package depends on `@pulumi/pulumi`.
The published `package.json` for SST's platform package depends on first-party Pulumi providers for AWS, Cloudflare, Docker builds, and more.
The published `package.json` for SST's platform package depends on a Pulumiverse Vercel provider.
`sst deploy` reads the user's `sst.config.ts` and resolves SST's own components, and this step is SST's responsibility.
SST's components compile into Pulumi resource declarations, and this step is SST's responsibility.
The Pulumi engine diffs desired vs. actual state, builds a dependency graph, and orders operations.
Terraform-bridged providers translate each resource into cloud API calls, and this is handled by Pulumi's Terraform bridge.
State is written to an S3 bucket in the user's AWS account, self-hosted by SST rather than by Pulumi Cloud.
SST owns the developer-facing layer: the CLI, the component model, and the local dev loop.
Pulumi's engine owns the provisioning mechanics underneath SST: dependency resolution, preview and diff, state tracking, and the plumbing to hundreds of provider APIs.
AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types, each with its own create, update, and delete semantics.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge is Apache-2.0 licensed.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge is built specifically to let projects like SST reuse Terraform's ecosystem of providers, adapted for the Pulumi engine, instead of writing and maintaining their own.
Pulumi's engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.
Pulumi's Automation API works for teams embedding Pulumi programs inside their own tools the same way Pulumi's engine embeds without requiring a Pulumi account or Pulumi Cloud.
The same provider bridge that lets SST use Terraform providers also lets any Pulumi user consume Terraform providers directly.
Nitric is a cloud-agnostic application framework.
Nitric's own docs state: "all of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments."
Nitric's official providers are built directly on Pulumi's AWS, GCP, and Azure providers.
Defang deploys Docker Compose applications to the cloud.
Defang describes its Pulumi provider as taking "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`" to provision the result.
SST, Nitric, and Defang all expose a narrower, more opinionated interface to their users while relying on the Pulumi engine and its provider bridge underneath.
SST users are not Pulumi Cloud customers.
SST's state lives in the user's own S3 bucket, not in Pulumi's hosted service.
SST does not require a Pulumi account to work.
Most SST users never write a line of Pulumi code; they work entirely in SST's component model.
SST's constructs compile to Pulumi resources.
Resources that don't have a dedicated SST construct yet can still be defined directly in Pulumi and deployed as part of the same SST app.
SST's latest release, v4.17.1, went out in July 2026.
The `sst` package on npm is pulling roughly 796,000 downloads a week as of this writing.
SST's own team page credits the same team behind opencode.
opencode is an open source AI coding agent.
opencode has grown quickly since launch.
opencode now carries a larger following on GitHub than SST itself.
SST's release cadence and download numbers indicate SST is not being abandoned.
SST's dependency on the Pulumi engine has not changed as a result of the team's broadened public attention.
If you already run SST, you are already running Pulumi's engine, whether or not you've written a line of Pulumi code yourself.
Pulumi Cloud provides cross-team visibility into infrastructure state.
Policy as code provides guardrails a platform team can enforce centrally.
Components allow sharing infrastructure patterns across a whole organization rather than just within one SST app.
Using Pulumi Cloud, policy as code, or components with an SST app does not require leaving the underlying Pulumi engine SST already uses.

Since SST v3 (the Ion rewrite, shipped mid-2024), `sst deploy` runs through an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls, replacing SST's earlier architecture on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
Pulumi's engine is embedded directly in the SST CLI.
SST keeps its own state in an S3 bucket in the user's AWS account rather than in Pulumi Cloud.
Users do not need to install Pulumi separately or create a Pulumi account to deploy an SST app.
SST's components are defined using Terraform providers, but those providers are bridged through the Pulumi engine rather than run through Terraform itself.
SST does not invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state.

Because SST's components compile into Pulumi resource declarations, users can define resources directly with Pulumi for anything that doesn't yet have a dedicated SST construct, and deploy them as part of the same app.
SST shipped v4.17.1 in July 2026.
The `sst` package continues to see roughly 796,000 weekly downloads on npm.
opencode has not changed SST's release cadence or its dependency on the Pulumi engine.

The `platform/package.json` in the `anomalyco/sst` repository (formerly `sst/sst`), verified September 2026, lists `@pulumi/pulumi`, `@pulumi/aws`, `@pulumi/cloudflare`, `@pulumi/command`, `@pulumi/docker-build`, `@pulumi/random`, `@pulumi/tls`, and `@pulumiverse/vercel` as direct dependencies.
The SST GitHub repository is now located at `anomalyco/sst`, formerly `sst/sst`.
npm download stats for `sst` show 796,291 downloads for the week of September 5-11, 2026.
The `anomalyco/opencode` repository's star count was observed on GitHub in September 2026.
